name: Minerva

attributes.attribute: a Romanized Celtic goddess of healing
unlike Athena, was no fighter save against disease and pain
linked to Belisama and to Sul of the Bath springs

sources: Green, Miranda. The Gods of Roman Britain. (Aylesbury: Shire Publications Ltd., 1983), 30.
Straffon, Cheryl. The Earth Goddess: Celtic and Pagan Legacy of the Landscape. London: Blandford, 1997, 24-29.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Minerva was a Romanized Celtic goddess of healing. In Rome she became the Greek warrior goddess Athena, but the Celtic Minerva was no fighter save against disease and pain. The Romans found many similar goddesses in Celtic lands whose healing power grew from the headwaters of rivers, hot springs, and other waters. One such goddess is carved into the Roman quarries near the River Dee in Chester. She wears an owl and a Gorgon's head, the symbols of the Greek Athena. Julius Caesar wrote that the Celtic Minerva taught arts and crafts to humanity, a claim the surviving images do not make clear. Sometimes the Romans kept the Celtic goddess's name. Other cases lost the name wholly. One Minerva, called Vitrix, the victor, appeared in reliefs as a helmet-crowned female head. Another was linked to Belisama, a warrior goddess. The most famous Celtic Minerva was Sul, the goddess of the hot springs at Bath in Britain.
